title: Uber's 2016 breach and its cover-up
hook: Hackers took millions of records; Uber paid them $100,000 and kept quiet for a year.
collected: Names, emails and phone numbers of riders and drivers; about 600,000 driver's licence numbers.
howObtained: Stored in Uber's cloud storage, accessed by intruders using credentials.
done: The FTC said Uber paid the intruders $100,000 through its bug-bounty programme and did not disclose the breach until November 2017, while the FTC was investigating it. Earlier, staff tools ('God View') had allowed broad access to riders' trips.
affected: More than 25 million names and emails, 22 million names and phone numbers, about 600,000 driver's licences (FTC).
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: FTC revised order. Uber's former security chief was later criminally convicted over the cover-up.

outcome.text: Expanded FTC order requiring breach reporting and regular assessments.

sources.title: Uber Agrees to Expanded Settlement with FTC

limits: The often-cited '57 million' is Uber's own combined figure.
whyItMatters: Data that is collected can be stolen. Keeping less data is a way to protect it.

title: 23andMe: relatives' DNA data exposed through other people's accounts
hook: About 6.9 million people were exposed, most through a 'DNA Relatives' feature, not their own passwords.
collected: Ancestry, relatives and some health-related genetic reports.
howObtained: Customers' saliva samples; data shown to relatives through matching features.
done: Attackers reused leaked passwords (credential stuffing) to enter some accounts, then scraped relatives' information through DNA Relatives, exposing about 6.9 million people.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Company disclosure, regulator penalties and court settlements.

outcome.text: UK ICO fine of £2.31 million (June 2025); class settlement revised to $46.75 million in bankruptcy; a multistate attorney-general settlement (2026). The company filed for bankruptcy in March 2025 and was bought by TTAM (a nonprofit led by co-founder Anne Wojcicki).

whyItMatters: You cannot change your DNA like a password. And when a company is sold, its data is sold with it.

title: Star Health insurance data sold through Telegram chatbots
hook: Claim documents and medical histories were served up by bots on a messaging app.
collected: Names, ID documents, insurance claim files and medical details.
howObtained: Held by Star Health; the attacker claimed access to over 31 million records.
done: An attacker calling themselves 'xenZen' offered the data and ran Telegram chatbots that returned customers' documents. The attacker claimed the company's own security chief sold it the data.
label: REPORTED
labelNote: Journalists verified sample documents. The insider claim is ALLEGED and was denied.

companyResponse.text: Star Health admitted "unauthorized and illegal access to certain data" and said its security chief "has not been found guilty" of any wrongdoing.
companyResponse.source: Star Health statements via The Register

outcome.text: Star Health won an interim court injunction (24 September 2024) against Telegram, Cloudflare and the attacker.

sources.title: Telegram argues against policing role in Star Health data breach case

limits: Total number affected and forensic findings not public.
whyItMatters: Health data collected for insurance ended up in strangers' hands.

title: Air India passenger data exposed through a vendor
hook: Ten years of passenger records leaked from a supplier most travellers have never heard of.
collected: Names, dates of birth, contact details, passport, ticket and frequent-flyer data (2011-2021).
howObtained: Stored by SITA, Air India's passenger-service system provider.
done: Air India disclosed that about 4.5 million passengers' data was affected in a breach at SITA.
label: DOCUMENTED

companyResponse.text: Air India said SITA did not hold card CVV numbers.

outcome.text: The same vendor breach affected other airlines.

sources.title: Air India says data breach impacts 4.5 million former passengers

whyItMatters: Your data lives with companies you have never chosen to deal with.

title: Juspay payment-gateway breach
hook: A backend payments company admitted a breach. The disagreement was over how many records.
collected: Masked card data, card fingerprints, emails and phone numbers.
howObtained: Stored by Juspay, which processes payments for many apps.
done: An attacker accessed Juspay systems in August 2020 using a developer access key. A researcher claimed 10 crore (100 million) records; Juspay said about 3.5 crore.
affected: Users of apps that pay through Juspay.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Company admitted the breach. The SIZE is CONTESTED.

companyResponse.text: Juspay called the 10-crore figure incorrect and said no full card numbers, PINs or passwords leaked.

sources.title: Juspay refutes 10 cr card data breach claim

whyItMatters: The payment layer behind your apps also holds your data.

title: BigBasket customer database offered for sale
hook: Addresses, phone numbers and dates of birth of about 2 crore grocery shoppers, the researchers said.
collected: Names, emails, password hashes, phones, addresses, dates of birth, location and login IP addresses.
done: Security firm Cyble reported a database of about 20 million BigBasket users for sale on the dark web.
label: REPORTED
labelNote: Security researchers' report. The company said it was evaluating the claim.

companyResponse.text: BigBasket said it was confident financial data was secure and was "evaluating the extent of the breach and authenticity of the claim", and filed a police complaint.

whyItMatters: Everyday apps hold a detailed map of your home life.

title: boAt customer data posted on a hacker forum
hook: Names and home addresses of millions of earphone buyers, a hacker claimed.
collected: Names, phones, emails, addresses and order IDs.
howObtained: Held by the company's online store.
done: A hacker claimed to post data on more than 7.5 million customers. TechCrunch said part of a sample appeared genuine.
label: REPORTED
labelNote: Journalists checked a sample. The total is the hacker's claim.

companyResponse.text: boAt said it was aware of claims regarding a potential data leak and was investigating.

sources.title: Indian audio giant boAt investigating data breach

limits: The 7.5 million figure comes from the hacker.
whyItMatters: Even a gadget shop's database is valuable to criminals.

title: The '375 million Airtel users' leak claim
hook: A hacker advertised a giant leak. Airtel denied it, and researchers thought it was recycled.
collected: Claimed: phones, emails, Aadhaar numbers and addresses.
done: A forum post offered data on 375 million Airtel users for $50,000. The forum removed it as a suspected scam; researchers suggested it combined older leaked datasets.
label: CONTESTED
labelNote: Seller's claim versus company denial; researchers lean towards recycled data.

companyResponse.text: Airtel called it "nothing short of a desperate attempt to tarnish Airtel's reputation by vested interests" and said there was no breach.

outcome.text: No evidence of a new breach found.

sources.title: India's Airtel dismisses data breach reports

limits: Old leaks resurface under new names.
whyItMatters: Teaches scepticism: not every 'mega-leak' is what it claims.

title: Domino's India order data leak claim
hook: Researchers claimed 18 crore orders leaked; the company confirmed an incident but not financial data.
collected: Claimed: names, phones, addresses and order details.
howObtained: Held by Jubilant FoodWorks (Domino's India franchise).
done: Researchers and sellers claimed about 180 million order records and 1 million cards were exposed.
label: CONTESTED
labelNote: Company confirmed a security incident but disputed that financial data leaked; the size is from researchers and sellers.

companyResponse.text: Jubilant FoodWorks confirmed an information security incident but said no financial information was accessed.

sources.title: Domino's data breach: Jubilant says no financial data leaked

whyItMatters: Company statements and outside claims often disagree.

title: MobiKwik KYC data leak claim
hook: Researchers claimed identity documents of about 10 crore users were on the dark web. The company denied it.
collected: Claimed: KYC (identity-verification) documents and card data.
done: Researchers claimed the data of about 100 million users was offered online. The RBI ordered a forensic audit.
label: CONTESTED
labelNote: Researchers' claim versus company denial; no public audit result found.

outcome.text: RBI directed a forensic audit by a CERT-In-empanelled auditor; no public result found.

sources.title: RBI directs MobiKwik to carry out forensic audit

whyItMatters: Without published audits, users cannot know what happened.

title: COVID-test records offered on a hacker forum
hook: Aadhaar and passport numbers of crores of Indians, a seller claimed, taken from COVID testing data.
collected: Names, phone numbers, addresses, Aadhaar and passport numbers.
howObtained: Claimed to come from ICMR COVID-19 testing data.
done: A seller claimed 815 million records. Security firm Resecurity checked samples against Aadhaar verification and found matches.
affected: Indians who took COVID tests (size claimed).
label: REPORTED
labelNote: Security researchers verified samples. The exact source (ICMR, NIC or the health ministry) is unknown.

companyResponse.text: No detailed public government response found; CERT-In reportedly alerted ICMR.

sources.title: 81.5 crore Indians' personal data leaked, claims hacker

whyItMatters: Data collected for public health became an identity-theft risk.

title: Ransomware takes down AIIMS Delhi's systems
hook: India's top public hospital went back to paper for about two weeks.
collected: Patient records and lab data on hospital servers.
done: A ransomware attack hit AIIMS Delhi's e-hospital servers. The government told Parliament five physical servers were affected.
label: DOCUMENTED
labelNote: Government confirmation in Parliament. Whether data was stolen was not confirmed.

companyResponse.text: AIIMS said e-hospital data had been restored and systems were being sanitised.

outcome.text: Police registered an extortion and cyber-terrorism case.

sources.title: Cyberattack on top Indian hospital highlights security risk

limits: Attribution to any country rests on police sources only.
whyItMatters: Over-centralised health data is a target.

title: A Telegram bot returned CoWIN vaccination details
hook: Type in a phone or Aadhaar number, get back someone's vaccination details.
collected: Names, ID numbers and vaccination details.
howObtained: Unclear: the government says it came from previously stolen data.
done: Journalists reported a Telegram bot that returned registration details for a given phone or Aadhaar number.
label: CONTESTED
labelNote: Journalists REPORTED the bot; the government disputes that CoWIN itself was breached.

companyResponse.text: The health ministry said CoWIN was not directly breached and called some reports "mischievous"; officials said the bot likely used previously stolen data.

outcome.text: CERT-In investigation; no public report found.

sources.title: Health ministry statement on CoWIN
sources.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Government of India

whyItMatters: When the source is disputed, both 'it was hacked' and 'it wasn't hacked' can mislead.

title: The Tribune buys access to Aadhaar details for ₹500
hook: A reporter paid ₹500 over WhatsApp for a login that showed anyone's Aadhaar details.
collected: Name, address, phone and photo linked to Aadhaar numbers.
howObtained: A misused login sold through WhatsApp, according to the report.
done: The Tribune reported buying access that returned details for any Aadhaar number entered.
label: REPORTED
labelNote: Investigative journalism (the reporter bought access). The authority says it was misuse, not a breach.

companyResponse.text: UIDAI said "there has not been any breach of biometric database", called the story misreporting, and filed a police complaint.

outcome.text: Police complaint filed; biometric data was not shown to be exposed.

whyItMatters: 'No breach' and 'misuse of access' can both be true at once.
